newsitem.title: NAMIBIA: Kabila's Congo seeks southern African support.
newsitem.headline: Kabila's Congo seeks southern African support.

text.p: The Democratic Republic of the Congo's cooperation minister Thomas Kanza said on Tuesday his country was seeking joint projects with southern African countries in mining, agriculture and energy.
"We have mines, we have agriculture, we have energy and we are prepared to cooperate with all our brothers (in southern Africa)," he told reporters during a visit to Windhoek.

He said the new Congo wanted the 12-member Southern African Development Community (SADC) to help rebuild his country's bankrupt economy after decades of dictatorship by ousted president Mobutu Sese Seseko.
Mobutu was toppled last month after a seven-month rebellion by the Alliance of Laurent Kabila, who is now president.
"We in the Congo consider ourselves being a lost brother of our brothers in southern Africa", Kanza, the Congo's Minister of International Cooperation said.
He said he hoped that by following the objectives of the SADC through formal and informal cooperation, the country would be able to prove its credibility as a partner in development.

The Congo has expressed interest in joining the SADC trade grouping which comprises South Africa, Zimbabwe, Namibia, Botswana, Mozambique, Angola, Zambia, Malawi, Tanzania, Lesotho, Swaziland and Mauritius.
Kanza is on a week-long tour of Angola, Zimbabwe and Zambia.
He said under Mobutu, Zaire had been unable to join SADC.
"But now we are happy to join our brothers. We are going to develop Africa and the African people", he said.
He said the repayment of debt would have to take a backseat as the Kabila government tried to rebuild the country and provide food and medicine to its people.
It also needed to pay the salaries of its civil service who have not been paid for 18 months.
Kanza said Namibia would serve as a model in trying to follow up stability with development.

Namibia's foreign minister Theo Ben Gurirab reiterated his support for Kabila's new Congo, saying apart from democracy and historical ties, the wealth of natural resources the Congo had to offer could benefit regional development.
